hints: The unbiased estimate of the population mean is the sample mean: $\dfrac{\sum t}{n}$ with $\sum t = 560$ and $n = 40$.
For the variance, use the unbiased formula that divides by $n - 1$: $s^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1}\left(\sum t^2 - \dfrac{(\sum t)^2}{n}\right)$, with $\sum t^2 = 7850$.
Work out $\dfrac{560^2}{40}$ first, subtract it from $7850$, then divide by $39$. If you divide by $40$ you get the biased estimate and lose the marks.
walkthrough:
**What 'unbiased estimate' means**

We only have a sample of 40 races, but we want to estimate the mean $\mu$ and the variance $\sigma^2$ of all Tania's races. An 'unbiased' estimate is one that is right on average, not too high or too low.

**Estimate of $\mu$ (B1)**

The unbiased estimate of the population mean is the sample mean.

$$\hat{\mu} = \bar{t} = \frac{\sum t}{n} = \frac{560}{40} = 14$$

**Estimate of $\sigma^2$ (M1)**

The unbiased estimate of the variance divides by $n - 1$, not $n$:

$$s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\left(\sum t^2 - \frac{(\sum t)^2}{n}\right) = \frac{1}{39}\left(7850 - \frac{560^2}{40}\right)$$

Why $n - 1$: the sample values cluster closer to their own mean than to the true mean, so dividing by $n$ would give an answer that is too small on average. Dividing by $n - 1$ corrects that.

**Calculate (A1)**

Square first: $560^2 = 313\,600$. Divide by $40$: $\dfrac{313\,600}{40} = 7840$.

$$7850 - 7840 = 10$$$$s^2 = \frac{10}{39} = 0.25641\ldots$$

The other form from the scheme gives the same thing: $\dfrac{40}{39}\left(\dfrac{7850}{40} - 14^2\right) = \dfrac{40}{39}\left(196.25 - 196\right) = \dfrac{40}{39} \times 0.25 = \dfrac{10}{39}$.

Slip to avoid: leaving out the $\dfrac{40}{39}$ (or dividing by $40$) gives $0.25$, which is the biased value, and scores no marks.

**Final answer**

Unbiased estimate of $\mu$ is $14$.

Unbiased estimate of $\sigma^2$ is $\dfrac{10}{39} = 0.256$ (3 s.f.; the scheme also shows $0.25641$).

hints: '$S$ is at least $0.1$ more than $T$' means $S - T \geqslant 0.1$. Set up the new variable $S - T$ and find its mean using $14.2$ for $S$ and your estimate of $\mu$ for $T$: $\text{E}(S - T) = \text{E}(S) - \text{E}(T)$.

The races are independent, so the variances **add** even though you subtract the variables: $\text{Var}(S - T) = \text{Var}(S) + \text{Var}(T)$, using $0.3$ and your estimate of $\sigma^2$ from part (a).
$S - T$ is normal. Standardise the boundary $0.1$ using the mean and variance you just found: $z = \dfrac{0.1 - \text{E}(S-T)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(S-T)}}$.
You want $\text{P}(S - T > 0.1)$, the **upper** tail, so the probability is $1 - \Phi(z)$.
Your $z$ will be negative, so find $\Phi$ of it with the calculator (or use $1 - \Phi(z) = \Phi(-z)$). The answer should be a little over $0.5$, because the boundary is below the mean. Give 3 s.f.
walkthrough:
**Turn the question into one variable**

We want 'Suki's time at least $0.1$ s more than Tania's', that is $S - T \geqslant 0.1$. Because $S$ and $T$ are independent and normal, the difference $D = S - T$ is also normal. We need its mean and variance.

$$\text{P}(D \geqslant 0.1) = \text{P}(S - T \geqslant 0.1)$$

**Mean of $D$ (first B1 ft)**

From part (a), $T$ has mean (estimated) $14$. Suki's mean is $14.2$. The mean of a difference is the difference of the means.

$$\text{E}(D) = 14.2 - 14 = 0.2$$

**Variance of $D$ (second B1 ft)**

For independent variables, $\text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2\,\text{Var}(X) + b^2\,\text{Var}(Y)$. With $a = 1$ and $b = -1$, we get $(-1)^2 = 1$, so the variances **add**. Subtracting variables never subtracts variances.

$$\text{Var}(D) = 0.3 + \frac{10}{39} = 0.3 + 0.25641 = 0.55641$$

(The scheme uses $0.256$ and gets $0.55641$ as well, and accepts $\dfrac{217}{390}$.)

$$D \sim \text{N}(0.2,\ 0.55641)$$

**Standardise (first M1)**

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance: $\sqrt{0.55641} = 0.74593$.

$$z = \frac{0.1 - 0.2}{0.74593} = \frac{-0.1}{0.74593} = -0.134$$

**Choose the correct area (second M1)**

We want the probability that $D$ is **bigger** than $0.1$, which is the area to the right of $z = -0.134$.

$$\text{P}(D > 0.1) = 1 - \Phi(-0.134)$$

By symmetry of the normal curve, $1 - \Phi(-0.134) = \Phi(0.134)$.

**Evaluate (A1)**

$\Phi(0.134)$: normal table or calculator normal cdf $\to 0.5533$.

Quick check: the boundary $0.1$ is slightly below the mean $0.2$, so more than half of the probability is above it. $0.553$ fits.

If you used the biased variance, you would get $0.554$, which the scheme still accepts for the A1.

**Final answer**

The probability that Suki's time is at least $0.1$ s more than Tania's is $0.553$ (3 s.f.).
